units: the writer of the message answers a question about what he does
a first workshop teaches him to shape hollow figures in clay
the trainer finds his movements still too hurried
a second room is used for moulding and smells of damp material
the writer smooths surfaces there for whole afternoons
one space is given over to making jointed puppets
the back room takes the rehearsals and heats up under its lamp
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see for himself
text: You asked what on earth I get up to at the arts centre, so here is the whole list. The clay workshop comes first. I am learning to shape hollow figures there, and the trainer keeps telling me my hands are far too hurried. Next along is the moulding room, which smells of damp plaster and has buckets lined up against the wall. I spend entire afternoons in there, rubbing surfaces down until they feel soft under the palm. Then comes the puppet corner: heads carved out of soft wood, painted eyes, tiny clothes stitched by hand. Last of all, the back room takes the stage rehearsals, and the lamp above it throws off so much heat that we open the window between scenes. I never expected to grow fond of a place like this, and now I cannot bear to miss a session. Come and join me one afternoon, and you will see it all at once.

units: a restoration specialist is questioned about a damaged painting
she saw the poor state of the work as soon as it arrived
the yellowed protective layer flattened the pale colours
the work begins with a careful examination lasting several weeks
this examination finds the places where the painted matter is lifting
the cleaning moves forward in very small patches
the added retouches can be taken off and do not cover the original
the features of the face became readable again after a single sitting
the work is then put in a space where the damp is controlled
text: When did you realise the canvas was in danger? The restorer says she knew as soon as it came out of its wrapping: the varnish had yellowed so badly that the pale tones were flattened. Where does one begin in a case like that? With examination, she answers, several weeks of inspection under a lens, noting every place where the painted layer is lifting. Cleaning follows, carried out patch by tiny patch, with swabs that are changed over and over. Then the retouching, which never covers the original: fine strokes are laid into the losses and can be taken off again. And did the outcome surprise you? She smiles and admits that the features of the face, long drowned in a brown haze, came back in a single sitting. What becomes of the work now? It goes behind glass, into a room where the damp is watched at all hours.

units: a sculptor breaks off his work to question his pupil
the pupil finds that the block of stone resists her
each of her blows tears off a chip she did not intend
the master explains that stone holds veins running in one direction
striking across those veins shatters the surface
he advises drawing the shape in charcoal first
he recommends taking the matter away in layers while going round the block
the pupil finds this way of working exhausting
the next day the shape comes on and the chipping has stopped
text: The sculptor set down his mallet and asked why the work had gone quiet. His pupil answered that the block was fighting her, since every blow she struck tore off a flake she had never intended. He told her that stone runs in veins, and that striking a vein at an angle will shatter the whole face of it. Because she cut without listening to the grain, the material took its revenge. Draw the outline in charcoal, he said, then take the stone off in thin layers, walking round the block as you go. She objected that working so slowly wore her out. The sculptor smiled. Stone forgives nothing you remove from it, he said, so haste costs more than patience ever does. She picked up her chisel and made no reply. The next day she reported that the flaking had stopped and the shape was rising at last. He nodded without lifting his eyes, for he had heard it coming in the ring of the metal.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: reproducing pictures once called for a draughtsman for every copy
two copies made by hand were never alike
cutting a metal plate settled this failure of fidelity
the ink held in the grooves passes onto the paper under pressure
hollowing the metal with a burin took weeks and a skilled hand
the plate was then covered with a protection and the metal bitten with acid
a light point was enough from then on to open the line
this method made the line suppler and the tones came from the density of the cuts
text: Getting pictures about ran into a physical limit: every copy called for a draughtsman's hand, and no two copies made that way ever matched. Engraving settled the difficulty. A polished metal plate was cut with a burin, charged with stiff ink, then wiped clean, so that only what stayed in the grooves passed onto the sheet under the press. Fidelity was answered, but a fresh trouble came with it, for cutting copper took weeks and a very steady hand. The idea arose of biting the metal with acid instead, under a coat of varnish through which a light needle was enough to trace. A draughtsman who was clumsy with the burin could now print his own line. Contours grew suppler, tone was built up from the density of the hatching, and the picture at last travelled far away from the person who had made it.

units: two separate methods serve to decorate a wall
the first means painting on a coating that is still wet
the colour sets into the lime as it dries
the painter has a single sitting before the surface hardens
his drawing is settled beforehand and carried over from a pierced model
the second method sets coloured fragments into a mortar
the craftsman can break off and take the work up again later
rounded shapes are built there in very small steps
both techniques stand up to damp but decay in different ways
text: Two separate methods share the decoration of walls, and neither asks the same movements or the same patience of its maker. The first is laid onto a coating that is still wet. The colour sinks into the lime and sets there as the surface dries, so the painter has one sitting and no more before everything hardens. The drawing must therefore be settled in advance, then carried over from a sheet pricked with holes. The second method rests on coloured fragments set one by one into a bed of mortar. Nothing presses here: the craftsman breaks off and takes the work up again the following week without harm. Against that, the curve of a face has to be built in minute steps, and a soft gradation is paid for in endless cutting. Damp troubles neither of them, yet one ages by growing pale and the other by shedding its pieces.

units: a group of amateur singers rehearses in an abandoned industrial building
the place brings them three separate discoveries
low sounds hang on there under the iron roof frame
the woman in charge has to slow her entry signals because of that echo
a single lamp leaves half the group in shadow
the singers at the back go by ear without seeing the beat
passers-by come in, listen to one piece and leave in silence
a regular audience forms without any invitation
the group finally chooses to perform there and not in the planned room
text: An amateur choir was rehearsing in a disused factory hall, and the place had three surprises in store for it. The first was acoustic: under the iron roof beams the low voices hung on for a whole second, which forced the conductor to slow every entry she gave. The second was visual. A single lamp, hooked to a girder, cut the group into two halves, one of them lit and the other drowned in shadow; the singers at the back learned to sing without seeing the beat and trusted their ears instead. The third surprise came from the neighbourhood. Passers-by wandered in, sat down on upturned crates, listened to one piece, then left without a word. By the close of the season the hall held a regular audience that nobody had invited, and the choir chose to give its concert there rather than in the room booked for it.

units: the soft plate is warmed first so that it hollows out easily
the design is drawn and then gone over in ink so as not to vanish
the broad zones are taken away with the thickest tool
the tool must be pushed away from the hand holding the plate
the details are opened with a fine tool
the rough edges are smoothed once the relief is there
the ink is spread with a roller until it makes a steady noise
the sheet is rubbed from behind with a smooth curved object
one corner is lifted to check the result before the sheet is taken off
text: Take a plate of lino and let it warm up beside a radiator, because warm material gives way under the tool instead of fighting back. Draw your design in soft pencil, then go over the lines in ink, or you will lose the outline with the very first shaving. Clear the broad areas with the widest gouge you have, pushing away from your free hand. Move on to the fine gouge for the details, the hatching, the edges of each shape. Once the relief looks clean to you, sand the furry ridges down a little. Spread the ink on a sheet of glass, load the roller until it gives a steady hiss, then ink the block, crossing your passes as you go. Lay the paper on, rub the back with the curved bowl of a spoon, and lift one corner to check. If the tone looks thin, drop the sheet back and work at it again before you take it off.

units: a local performance venue reopens after three winters of closure
cracks in the vault had at first raised the fear of destruction
the survey concluded that the structure was sound
damp was rising from the foundations and eating into the ornaments
the work was turned towards drying out and glueing the decorations back
the company was able to rehearse in the entrance hall during the work
the neighbourhood took to attending those rehearsals
every seat of the season is sold on reopening
the management explains this turnaround by the constant presence of the actors
text: Shut for three winters, a neighbourhood theatre has just reopened, and its return rests on a decision the management long hesitated to take. Cracks in the vaulted ceiling had at first raised the fear of demolition. The survey found instead that the structure was holding, but that damp was rising through the foundations and eating into the plaster ornaments. The work therefore changed its aim: rather than build the auditorium anew, the team dried it out and glued the mouldings back one by one. That turn had an effect nobody had foreseen. Since the craftsmen were on site throughout, the company could rehearse in the entrance hall, and the neighbourhood took to coming in to watch. On reopening night the whole season was sold out, though the theatre had shut its doors in front of empty rows. The management puts the reversal down to the actors being there all along.

units: a dirty glass roof leaves the studio in a dull light
this setting falsifies every colour laid on the canvas
the painter only finds her mistakes by taking the picture outside
she gives up opening a bay in the back wall because the stones are too thick
the bulbs she tries give a yellow cast that is worse still
she puts a broad tilted mirror on the opposite wall
the outside light thrown back by that mirror reaches the easel without hardness
she now begins her drawing as soon as the studio opens
her colours hold good once the picture hangs elsewhere
text: Under its grimy glass roof, the studio lay in a dull grey light that took the life out of every tone she laid down. The painter complained of it each winter: her blues turned to ash, her reds lost their warmth, and she found her mistakes out only by carrying the canvas outdoors. She thought of cutting an opening in the back wall, but the stonework proved far too thick for that. She tried harsh bulbs, whose yellow cast looked worse still. The answer came to her from a mirror. She fixed a broad panel of it against the opposite wall, tilted towards the floor, and the daylight it threw back spread over the easel at last with no hardness in it. Since then she starts drawing as soon as the shutters are open, and her colours hold to their promise when the canvas hangs somewhere else.

units: the writer holds it wrong to treat an image file as the work itself
this confusion weighs on the budgets of collections
a photograph gives the outlines and the values if the lighting is set
it does not give back the thickness or the relief of the painted matter
the look of a protective layer changes with where the viewer stands
a file depends on a format, on a support and on a reading program
each of those parts ends up unusable
a print kept in a folder can be looked at with no device
the writer grants that the digital copy protects the original and carries it far
the writer concludes that the copy documents the work without replacing it
text: To set an image file beside the work it records is to muddle two objects of a different nature, and collections pay dearly for the muddle. A photograph gives back the outlines, the values, often the hue, provided the lighting has been calibrated. What escapes it is the thickness of the matter: the ridge of a loaded brushstroke, the grain of the paper, the depth of a varnish that answers the eye afresh with every step the viewer takes. The file ages worse than people suppose; it hangs on a format, on a magnetic support, on a program able to read it, and every one of those links falls out of use. A print forgotten in a folder can be read again with no device at all. Should the digital copy be refused, then? No: it spares the original from handling and carries the image where nobody will travel. But it documents a work, it does not replace it.
